standard.title: 2D Representations of 3D Objects
standard.description: represent objects in 2 dimensions; discuss and reason about the advantages and disadvantages of different representations
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can compare parallel cross-sections and recognise their relationship to right prisms (from AC9M6SP01). Students have informal experience with drawings of 3D objects.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students represent 3D objects using nets, isometric drawings, and plan/elevation views, and reason about the advantages and disadvantages of each representation.

nodes.label: Nets of prisms and other 3D objects
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students identify, draw and construct nets of prisms and other common 3D objects.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify which nets will fold to make a cube or rectangular prism; draw a net for a triangular prism.
nodes.typical_width: Test multiple possible nets for the same object; identify which are valid; construct 3D objects from nets.
wider: Investigate how many valid nets a cube has (11) — systematically find them all.
Design and construct nets for less familiar solids (square pyramid, cylinder).

response_modes.reason: Students develop spatial reasoning for nets by working with multiple 3D objects. Restricting practice to cubes gives a false sense of mastery that fails with other prisms.

success_criteria: Correctly identifies valid nets for a cube and rectangular prism.
Draws a net that folds correctly to produce a given 3D object.
Does not include overlapping faces in a net.

nodes.label: Isometric and plan/elevation drawings
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students draw and interpret isometric drawings and plan/elevation views (front, back, side, top) of 3D objects.
nodes.minimum_width: Construct at least two views (e.g. top and front) of a given 3D object; interpret an isometric drawing.
nodes.typical_width: Draw all standard views of a given object; build an object from its views; use isometric paper to draw 3D objects.
wider: Interpret aerial/isometric views of real buildings or structures and identify the 3D object they represent.
Investigate 2D representations in First Nations Australian art — discuss what spatial information is conveyed.

response_modes.reason: Interpreting and drawing 2D representations of 3D objects requires systematic reasoning: which face is visible from each view? Students who proceed intuitively produce inconsistent views.

nodes.hinge_reason: Students who produce inconsistent views cannot reason about representation trade-offs in Node 3 — they cannot evaluate whether a net or isometric view is more useful without being able to correctly produce and read both.
success_criteria: Correctly draws at least two views of a 3D object.
Reconstructs a 3D object from its views.
Does not confuse view orientation (e.g. top vs front).

nodes.label: Advantages and disadvantages of different representations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students reason about when each type of 2D representation is most useful and what information each preserves or loses.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one advantage and one disadvantage of using a net vs an isometric drawing for the same object.
nodes.typical_width: Compare representations for a range of objects and purposes; match the representation to the task (e.g. net for construction, isometric for communication).
wider: Investigate professional contexts: architects use plans, packaging designers use nets, engineers use orthographic views — discuss why.
Evaluate: which representation best communicates a given 3D design decision?

response_modes.reason: Reasoning about representation trade-offs requires familiarity with all representation types simultaneously — this node integrates the prior two nodes.

success_criteria: States at least one advantage and one disadvantage for two different representations.
Selects an appropriate representation for a given purpose and justifies the choice.
Recognises that no single representation shows all information about a 3D object.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Reasoning about representation trade-offs in professional contexts (architecture, packaging, engineering) offers advancing students genuine applied spatial thinking — selecting and justifying the best representation for a purpose is a rich design task.
